questions.question: Which claim is most suitable for a structured debate?
choices: The city should extend library hours on school nights because student access is limited
Libraries are buildings
Everyone has an opinion about books
The city has many streets

questions.question: What makes a reason different from evidence?
choices: A reason is always a quotation
A reason explains why a claim may be true; evidence supports the reason
Evidence is a personal preference
They are identical terms

questions.question: A debater cites a survey of 800 local residents. What should the audience ask to evaluate it?
choices: What color the survey used
Whether the survey title is catchy
How participants were selected and what question they answered
How many pages the debate has

questions.question: Why address a counterclaim?
choices: To weaken the main claim without explanation
To avoid presenting evidence
To change the topic
To show that opposing reasoning has been considered and respond to it

questions.question: Which response best challenges an argument respectfully?
choices: The data support a different conclusion because they include only one season
Your argument is ridiculous
You clearly did not read the prompt
No one should listen to you

questions.question: A debater uses an emotional story as the only support for a broad policy claim. What is the main limitation?
choices: Stories can never be relevant evidence
One example may not establish how common the situation is
Policies cannot be discussed with examples
Emotion always makes reasoning invalid

questions.question: Which evidence most directly supports a claim about reduced traffic injuries after a street redesign?
choices: A drawing of the new street
A resident's favorite color
Comparable injury records from before and after the redesign
A list of unrelated city projects

questions.question: What is a rebuttal?
choices: A topic sentence introducing a new subject
A list of sources with no claim
An opening greeting
A response that challenges or answers an opposing argument

questions.question: A speaker says, 'My opponent wants children to be unsafe.' The opponent had argued only about budget. What tactic is this?
choices: Misrepresenting the opposing position
Providing a qualified concession
Using a direct comparison
Citing relevant evidence

questions.question: Which statement is a concession?
choices: The plan has no possible drawback
Although the plan costs more initially, it may reduce repair expenses later
My opponent's evidence is fabricated
Only one option exists

questions.question: A claim relies on a study from another country with different conditions. What should a debater explain?
choices: Why location never affects evidence
Why the study's title proves the claim
How well that evidence applies to the local situation
Why no other evidence is needed

questions.question: Which debate rule best supports fair participation?
choices: Allow only one side to ask questions
Reward interruptions
Change the rules during a speaker's turn
Set clear speaking turns and equal time limits

questions.question: An argument includes a claim, relevant evidence, and reasoning connecting them. What is strengthened by this structure?
choices: The audience can follow how the evidence supports the claim
The argument becomes automatically correct
The need to consider counterevidence disappears
The speaker no longer needs a conclusion

questions.question: Which question tests whether a source is relevant to a claim?
choices: Is the source's font attractive?
Does this source provide information that bears directly on the issue?
Is the source longer than the speech?
Does the source agree with my first impression?

questions.question: A debater cites a percentage but not the total number of people surveyed. What context is missing?
choices: The argument's topic
The speaker's speaking time
The sample size
The debate's location

questions.question: Why should a debater distinguish correlation from causation?
choices: Correlations cannot be measured
Causes are always opinions
The distinction applies only to history
A relationship between two trends alone does not prove one caused the other

questions.question: A team changes its position after hearing stronger evidence. What does that demonstrate?
choices: Evidence-based reasoning can lead to a revised claim
The team has lost automatically
Debate positions can never change
The earlier evidence should be hidden

questions.question: Which closing best fits a debate speech?
choices: Introduce an unrelated issue
Restate the central claim and summarize the strongest reasons and evidence
Add an unsupported statistic
Repeat the opening word for word

questions.question: A debater uses a personal attack instead of answering evidence. What is the problem?
choices: Personal attacks make evidence stronger
The opposing claim is therefore false
The attack does not address whether the opposing claim is supported
The audience cannot evaluate any claims

questions.question: What is the best way to compare two proposed policies?
choices: Use strong evidence for one and anecdotes for the other
Compare only their names
Ignore trade-offs
Use the same criteria and relevant evidence for both
